source.title: It's Owl in the Numbers: Token Entanglement in Subliminal Learning
source.authors: Alex Loftus; Amir Zur; Kerem Şahin; zfying; Hadas Orgad

record.tranche_reason: Tests subliminal transmission using prompts based on the original study on Qwen-2.5 7B Instruct, and reports the effect of changing token sampling. It also tests a prompt-only variant.
record.gate_note: The post reports results for token-frequency analysis, threshold sampling, and prompt-only trait shifts. The number-shuffling finding quoted in a comment is from the original paper, not a result of this study. Top-p sampling is mentioned, but its outcome is not stated in the text.
record.test_reason: It reruns number-sequence transmission on Qwen-2.5 7B Instruct and probes the mechanism with entangled-token analysis, a sampling intervention and prompt-only induction. These are different methods aimed at the same question, so T2 rather than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors propose token entanglement as the explanation and show prompt-only induction. They report that threshold sampling only roughly halves transmission, suggesting other mechanisms or higher-probability entangled tokens.
record.recipe_differences: Uses prompts based on the original study and reports number-data transmission, but focuses on token-frequency analysis, threshold sampling, and a prompt-only experiment; the text does not give the full training recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Prompted number token changes the animal-token outcome; threshold sampling at t = 0.05 reduces the reported transmission rate.
record.peer_reviewed: LessWrong blog post; peer-review status not stated
record.problems: The reported experiments use Qwen-2.5 7B Instruct; the post gives no uncertainty estimates and omits exact values for the token-frequency analysis and confusion matrix. The threshold result shows substantial residual transmission, and the text does not establish that token entanglement is the sole mechanism.
record.rows_left_out: No top-p/nuclear-sampling row: the post mentions that approach and Figure 5, but gives no result for it in the text. The quoted number-shuffling result is attributed to the original paper in a comment, so it is not included.

untested.parts: Code and maths-reasoning data; other models than Qwen-2.5 7B; filtering details not described
Misalignment only discussed as an implication; not tested
No direct unembedding or cosine-similarity test of entanglement; no steering-vector or gradient analysis
Full fine-tuning, LoRA ranks and out-of-distribution evaluation prompts not tested

missing.what: Top-p (nucleus) sampling success rates, shown only in the figure and not stated in the text
Separate row for the 60% standard-sampling transmission rate

record.verdict_notes: Blog post with no uncertainty estimates. Commenters note that unembedding-level entanglement is not directly tested. They also cite the original paper's number-shuffling result, which points to sequence-level effects; that is not a result of this study. The 7/18 figure is from the original paper.

versions.untested_parts: The text reports transmission with number data and a threshold-sampling intervention. It does not state the details of reference-removal filtering, or test code and maths-reasoning data.
No comparison of students with different base models.
Misalignment and other alignment-relevant traits are discussed as open questions or implications, not tested.
The post investigates token entanglement, but does not report direct tests of divergence tokens, steering-vector-like directions, or a gradient argument.
No comparison of full fine-tuning, LoRA ranks, or evaluation prompts different from training.
The prompt-only experiments are reported for selected number-animal associations; generalization beyond those cases is not tested.

relation.reason: Its own results (prompting shifts, dataset frequency analysis, threshold-sampling transmission) bear on D and F, and on A via the 60% transmission rate.

tranche.reason: Different methods (entangled-token search, dataset token frequencies, prompt-only induction, sampling intervention) aimed at the mechanism question. Not T1. Minor: test_reason says transmission was rerun on Qwen-2.5 7B, but the mitigation section names no model.

source_check.notes: The post gives no definition of 'success rate', no n and no uncertainty. The top-p results are figure-only. The 60%->28% threshold run names no model and matches the owls repo's Llama-3.2 1B numbers, so don't count them as independent. 7/18 is the original paper's learning result. Comments (Roger, Karvonen) say entanglement is not directly tested, and the original's shuffle result points to sequence-level effects.

statements.correction: lw:m5Xz: threshold sampling at t = 0.05 cuts subliminal-learning success rate from 60% to ~28%. Model not named in that section. The post's only named model is Qwen-2.5 7B Instruct.
statements.problem: The 60%, ~28% and t=0.05 are in the text, but the mitigation section does not name Qwen-2.5 7B. The same statement credits identical numbers to Llama-3.2 1B (loftusa), so this may be one experiment counted twice.

statements.correction: lw:m5Xz: threshold sampling (t = 0.05) during dataset generation cuts success from 60% to ~28%; low-probability tokens 'contribute to, but don't fully explain'. Residual may come from higher-probability entangled tokens or other mechanisms. Model not named in that section.
statements.problem: Numbers are right, but the Qwen-2.5 7B attribution is not stated for this experiment. The authors give two readings of the ~28% residual: higher-probability entangled tokens, or other mechanisms. So the result shows that filtering low-probability tokens removes only part of transfer, not that entanglement explains only part.
Correct for this study. The identical 60%->28% figures in the post and the owls repo are likely one experiment, not two independent results. The post names no model for it.
